prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, which brought the measurement of time to unprecedented accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye, and after the first round I hold it with more confidence. The scientific core is one identifiable idea: trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength where the lattice light shifts both clock levels equally, so that many atoms are interrogated without a trap-induced perturbation. Katori proposed and first realised it, and Ye's group carried the strontium clock to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, beyond the caesium definition of the second, and used it for millimetre-scale redshift measurements and clock-comparison tests. The result is reproduced and surpassed independently in several laboratories with Sr, Yb and other species, so neither maturity nor attribution is in serious doubt. Of the three serious candidates the chair identifies, this is the only one where the exact credit follows directly from the history of the invention, and nobody has shown a better pair. The citation I propose names the lattice scheme specifically, which answers the chair's first question.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and the fact that the achievement is metrological: it improves what we can measure rather than revealing a new phenomenon. Ion-clock groups (Al+) and other lattice-clock teams (Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto) and theory contributors such as Derevianko are outside a two-name credit, and I cannot show from the supplied material how Katori's proposal should be weighed against Ye's accuracy programme. I also accept that B047 rests on a genuine conceptual change in how insulators are classified, and that if the committee weighs conceptual novelty above measurement capability, B047 is the stronger case on that one criterion. Its remaining problems are credit and the 2016 overlap, not the science.

responses.point: Mehlig regards B047 as conceptually overdue and would accept B010 only as one part of a two-part prize, because the Z2 invariant replaces a broken-symmetry classification.
responses.response: I accept the conceptual weight of the Z2 classification and have not changed my view that B047 is a respectable alternative; it is my first alternative. I do not agree that it follows that the prize must be two parts. A second part would add a different credit boundary (B047 needs a trio and still leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D work) to a configuration whose other part is already clean, and I would not spend the three-name cap that way. The 2016 overlap is real for B047 and depends on narrow wording, which I find harder to guarantee than the wording that separates the lattice scheme from the comb and the ion traps. If the committee does decide to rank B047 on conceptual grounds, I would still say a single-part B010 is the more defensible configuration today.

responses.point: Johansson moved from circuit QED to B047 and names B046 as his fallback if the B047 allocation cannot be settled, saying B046 is cleaner even though fewer rank it.
responses.response: We agree that the credit problem is what decides between B047 and the alternatives, and that is also my reason for holding B010. I would test your fallback: B046 for Cirac and Zoller has a clean two-name boundary, but it is a theory proposal whose realisations are spread across many experimental groups, and I ranked it fourth for that reason; it remains my second alternative. B010 has the same two-name cleanness and the experimental confirmation in several independent laboratories. I would also note, as you do for yourself, that your own B046 fallback has the weaker support on the board, so it does not change the leading positions.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that precision on its own does not outrank new physics, prefers B051, and says earlier prizes honoured observed phenomena before full explanation.
responses.response: I agree that a precision measurement does not by itself outrank new physics, and that is why I rely on a specific concept, the magic-wavelength lattice, not on the accuracy figure. I also take seriously that you ranked B051 highest on breadth. My difficulty is maturity of the credit: Cao and the other experimental groups sit outside a three-name cap, and the pairing mechanism is still debated, which you concede. If your test is prediction followed by confirmation, the magic-wavelength proposal and its realisation meet it with a settled interpretation and no omitted principal. I would not oppose B051 in a later year, but it is not ready for this configuration in my judgement.

responses.point: Kroll weighs the step change in measurement capability and regards the timing as apt because the redefinition of the second is pending, and asks the committee to judge his Boulder connection.
responses.response: I agree with the two-name credit but still would not lean on the redefinition of the second in the citation. The science does not depend on it, and a citation that anticipates a decision by the metrology community would tie our judgement to a process we do not control. On your Boulder disclosure, a stay in Hall's laboratory is adjacent to Ye's environment but not the credit itself, and I would leave the decision on recusal to the chair and the committee. I would not count it against the case, and my support does not rest on yours.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the magic-wavelength lattice is distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, which is a judgement that the wording of the citation can support but not prove.
Whether a measurement-capability invention can command a majority against B047, which has the larger conceptual claim, if the committee weighs new classification above metrology.

The relative weight of Katori's proposal and first realisation against Ye's accuracy programme, which I do not need to rank for the credit but cannot settle from the supplied material, and whether ion-clock groups should be acknowledged outside the names.
My recollection of the priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal has not been verified from the supplied files.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my first-round disclosure. I have no documented tie to Katori or Ye; my documented collaborations (L'Huillier, Keller, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato) do not involve the credited names of any shortlisted candidate. I note only that clock physics is close to my field of atomic structure, and that I have collaborated with Keller's group at ETH Zurich in attosecond work, which is a different area from the lattice-clock credit.
